blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait for the shuttle or walk. The pilot data shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These counts track trips, not unique students, meaning one person could account for multiple boardings in a single week. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase does not prove that more students attended class. It only suggests that the trips taken during the pilot week were more frequent. The weeks also differed in academic schedule without randomization, which complicates any direct comparison. I am not asking for a conclusion about attendance; I am noting that the data measures usage frequency, not class presence. These figures cannot answer whether the shuttle caused students to show up to lectures.

blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: The survey data carries its own limitations. Only 18 voluntary responses were collected, all from existing shuttle riders, with 14 reporting that they valued the later service [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses describe the preferences of people already on the bus, not the student body at large. A small, self-selected group cannot represent demand across all students, particularly those who chose not to ride. Without input from non-riders, the committee lacks evidence that the broader population would use or need extended hours. This gap means the survey confirms rider satisfaction but cannot establish whether extending service would attract new users. The observations justify asking who can use the shuttle, not assuming they already do.

blocks.heading: Recommendation
blocks.content: I would not recommend making the schedule permanent on the current evidence. The absence of attendance records [@lyra:1], along with the lack of cost and emissions data [@lyra:2], prevents any assessment of the service’s broader impact. The 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1] indicate activity but do not prove that later service increased classroom presence. Because we have not measured what we do not have, the pilot should extend for one term to resolve these unknowns. This extension is conditional: it serves to gather the missing data, not to confirm success. The goal is to test whether the service functions as expected before committing resources long-term.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase does not prove that more students attended class. It only suggests that the trips taken during the pilot week were more frequent. The weeks also differed in academic schedule without randomization, which complicates any direct comparison. I am not asking for a conclusion about attendance; I am noting that the data measures usage frequency, not class presence. These figures cannot answer whether the shuttle caused students to show up to lectures.

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

## Evidence

I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait for the shuttle or walk. The pilot data shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These counts track trips, not unique students, meaning one person could account for multiple boardings in a single week. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase does not prove that more students attended class. It only suggests that the trips taken during the pilot week were more frequent. The pilot period was not a controlled experiment. I am not asking for a conclusion about attendance; I am noting that the data measures usage frequency, not class presence. These figures cannot answer whether the shuttle caused students to show up to lectures.

The survey data carries its own limitations. Only 18 voluntary responses were collected, all from existing shuttle riders, with 14 reporting that they valued the later service [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses describe the preferences of people already on the bus, not the student body at large. A small, self-selected group cannot represent demand across all students, particularly those who chose not to ride. Without input from non-riders, the committee lacks evidence that the broader population would use or need extended hours. This gap means the survey confirms rider satisfaction but cannot establish whether extending service would attract new users. The observations justify asking who can use the shuttle, not assuming they already do.

## Recommendation

Because the observations justify asking who can use the shuttle, I would not recommend making the schedule permanent on the current evidence. The observed boarding counts indicate activity but do not prove that later service increased classroom presence, especially given the missing attendance records [@lyra:1]. The absence of cost and emissions data [@lyra:2] prevents any assessment of the service’s broader impact. Because we have not measured what we do not have, the pilot should extend for one term to resolve these unknowns. This extension is conditional: it serves to gather the missing data, not to confirm success. The goal is to test whether the service functions as expected before committing resources long-term.

During that extension term, the measurement plan must address the gaps in the current dataset. The previous survey relied on eighteen voluntary responses from shuttle riders, yet non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. This means the data describe only the people already using the service and cannot establish demand across all students. To fix this, the next phase requires reaching out to students who do not currently take the shuttle to understand their barriers and preferences. We also need to track attendance directly, since no attendance data were collected during the pilot [@lyra:1]. Without comparing boarding numbers to actual class presence, we cannot determine if the service changes behavior. I want the committee to hear from non-riders as well as those on the bus, so we base future decisions on a complete picture rather than a partial one.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait for the shuttle or walk. The pilot data shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These counts track trips, not unique students, meaning one person could account for multiple boardings in a single week. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase does not prove that more students attended class. It only suggests that the trips taken during the pilot week were more frequent. The pilot period was not a controlled experiment. I am not asking for a conclusion about attendance; I am noting that the data measures usage frequency, not class presence. These figures cannot answer whether the shuttle caused students to show up to lectures.

live_draft_blocks.content: The survey data carries its own limitations. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses describe the preferences of people already on the bus, not the student body at large. Without input from non-riders, the committee lacks evidence that the broader population would use or need extended hours. This gap means the survey confirms rider satisfaction but cannot establish whether extending service would attract new users. The observations justify asking who can use the shuttle, not assuming they already do.

The previous survey relied on eighteen voluntary responses from shuttle riders, yet non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. This means the data describe only the people already using the service and cannot establish demand across all students. To fix this, the next phase requires reaching out to students who do not currently take the shuttle to understand their barriers and preferences. We also need to track attendance directly, since no attendance data were collected during the pilot [@lyra:1]. Without comparing boarding numbers to actual class presence, we cannot determine if the service changes behavior. I want the committee to hear from non-riders as well as those on the bus, so we base future decisions on a complete picture rather than a partial one.
